content: Laboratory diagnostics, monitoring, evaluation, and drug and supply management systems are essential components of healthcare delivery. It is critical to establish clear standards of care for every level of the health system, including the private sector. Each level of the health system should operate within its capacity, with well-defined lines of authority and accountability. This process must be supported by a regulatory framework, including laws, regulations, policies, and guidelines, to enable various cadres of healthcare workers to perform specific tasks. Adaptations may also be necessary to address the needs of specific populations. HIV care and treatment services for pregnant and postpartum women, as well as HIV-exposed and infected children, can be effectively provided in decentralized settings. This approach is particularly beneficial in areas with a high burden of HIV, where many women and children access health services through primary care. In contrast, in settings with a low burden of HIV, a centralized service delivery model with strong community linkages may be more appropriate. In such cases, healthcare providers should design service delivery models that align with the values and preferences of these populations. This includes providing related services in the same settings, establishing systems for information sharing, and ensuring effective referrals across settings and providers. Integration of services can reduce missed opportunities for initiating ART, improve adherence support, and optimize retention in care. In generalized epidemic settings, ART should be initiated and maintained for pregnant and postpartum women and infants within maternal and child healthcare settings. These settings should also provide linkage and referral to ongoing HIV care and ART when appropriate. Since 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended initiating ART for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count, including pregnant and breastfeeding women. However, access to ART for these women remains a challenge, as does the provision of essential HIV services to HIV-exposed infants and the prevention of mother-to-child transmission, particularly for vulnerable groups such as adolescent girls, young women, female sex workers, and women who inject drugs. Maternal and child health settings provide a critical opportunity to offer ART, as many women living with HIV only access health services during pregnancy. In most generalized HIV epidemic settings, these services are delivered at the primary care level, where pregnant women and children predominantly seek care. WHO recommends offering HIV testing to pregnant women through provider-initiated approaches as part of maternal, newborn, and child health services. Couple and partner HIV testing is also recommended in maternal and child health settings in generalized HIV epidemics and should be considered for key populations in concentrated and low-level epidemics. In high-burden HIV settings, retesting during late pregnancy (third trimester) is advised for women with unknown or negative HIV status, with catch-up testing if initial tests are missed or delayed. Additional postpartum retesting may be considered in high-burden regions or for women at higher risk of HIV acquisition. ART should be readily available in maternal and child health clinics or through linked service delivery models. Pregnant women, regardless of when they start ART, may require more intensive monitoring of viral suppression, including viral load testing during late pregnancy or at delivery, to identify those at risk of treatment failure or perinatal transmission. Breastfeeding women should also undergo viral load testing three months postpartum and every six months thereafter to detect viremic episodes during the postnatal period. Not all maternal and child health settings can provide long-term HIV care and treatment for women, their partners, and infants. These settings must assess and determine the optimal timing for transitioning mothers and infants to chronic HIV care or back to maternal and child health services when the woman was already receiving ART at conception. Providing women living with HIV with the choice of where to receive ART care is important and should not compromise the quality and person-centered nature of antenatal care. In settings with a high burden of both HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated in TB treatment settings with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. Similarly, TB treatment may be provided for people living with HIV in HIV care settings if they are also diagnosed with TB. Integrating sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception, within HIV care settings is feasible and can lead to improved outcomes. Evidence suggests that integration increases the uptake of sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception, and may reduce stigma while improving service quality. However, integration must be carefully planned to avoid overburdening providers and compromising service quality. The integration of diabetes and hypertension care with HIV services is also recommended, particularly in lowand middle-income countries facing a growing burden of noncommunicable diseases. People living with HIV are at increased risk of noncommunicable diseases due to aging, modifiable risk factors, and ART-related side effects. Integrated care models may improve the management of both HIV and noncommunicable diseases, but implementation requires careful planning, community engagement, and support for healthcare providers. Finally, addressing barriers to service uptake, such as stigma, gender-based violence, and social exclusion, is essential for improving access to integrated care. Research is needed to identify effective strategies for integrating services, optimizing supply chains, and addressing the unique needs of people living with HIV and noncommunicable diseases.
